slides.heading: Optimal Freelancing
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Greedy Algorithms
slides.narration: Let's solve Optimal Freelancing, an easy greedy algorithms problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Each job takes one day and has a deadline (days left) and a payment.
Working at most 7 days, one job per day, maximise profit.
Greedy: take jobs by payment descending and place each in the latest free day on or before its deadline.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Each job takes one day and has a deadline (days left) and a payment. Working at most 7 days, one job per day, maximise profit. Greedy: take jobs by payment descending and place each in the latest free day on or before its deadline.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Greedy by payment: take the most valuable jobs first and schedule each as late as its deadline allows.
slides.narration: Greedy by payment: take the most valuable jobs first and schedule each as late as its deadline allows.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: try every subset and order of jobs → exponential
Greedy: highest pay first, as late as possible → O(n log n)
Scheduling late keeps early days free for tight deadlines
slides.narration: Brute force would try every subset and ordering. Instead, take jobs from highest pay to lowest and place each on the latest free day before its deadline. Placing late keeps early days open for jobs with tight deadlines.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Sort jobs by payment, highest first
2. Keep seven day slots
3. Place each job in the latest free day before its deadline
4. Sum the payments of placed jobs
slides.narration: Step by step. First, sort jobs by payment, highest first. Second, keep seven day slots. Third, place each job in the latest free day before its deadline. Fourth, sum the payments of placed jobs.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Job C (pay 2, deadline 3) → day 3; earned 2
slides.narration: Job C pays 2 with deadline 3. The latest free day on or before the deadline is day 3, so we book it. Earnings so far: 2.

slides.narration: Job D pays 2 with deadline 2. The latest free day on or before the deadline is day 2, so we book it. Earnings so far: 4.

slides.caption: Job A (pay 1, deadline 1) → day 1; earned 5
slides.narration: Job A pays 1 with deadline 1. The latest free day on or before the deadline is day 1, so we book it. Earnings so far: 5.

slides.narration: Job B pays 1 with deadline 2. Every day up to its deadline is taken, so we skip it. Earnings so far: 5.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We sort jobs by payment descending and keep a seven-slot boolean array. For each job, we scan backwards from its capped deadline for a free day, mark it, and add the payment.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(1) (7 slots)
slides.narration: Time is O of n log n. Space is constant (7 slots).

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Deadlines beyond 7 → cap at day 7
Equal payments: any order works
No jobs → 0
slides.narration: Cap deadlines at seven since the week only has seven days. With no jobs, the answer is zero.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Explain why 'as late as possible' matters
Follow-up: n days instead of 7 → union-find for free slots
slides.narration: Explain why scheduling late matters. With many days instead of seven, a union-find of free slots makes the search fast.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Greedy by payment: take the most valuable jobs first and schedule each as late as its deadline allows.
Complexity: O(n log n)
